tagline: A river climb links old-growth redwoods with a road beneath the summit.
intro: US 199 climbs steadily but curves through the Smith River National Recreation Area, following the Smith River and its Middle Fork through Six Rivers National Forest. Most of its California mileage forms the Smith River Scenic Byway, a National Forest Scenic Byway. The drive begins among the redwoods of Jedediah Smith Redwoods State Park and eventually passes beneath Hazel View Summit through Collier Tunnel.

Crescent City had no inland road when it incorporated in 1854. A company’s first attempt stalled during the Panic of 1855; revived in 1856, it opened a plank road in May 1858. Horace Gasquet began another road in 1881, connecting Gasquet Flats to the plank road near Oregon Mountain. California and Oregon completed a new Gasquet–Kerby highway in 1926, the year the US 199 designation arrived. In 1929, the new Hiouchi Bridge bypassed the remaining old road over Howland Hill.

From US 101 near Crescent City, head through the state park, over a ridge and across the Smith River. Hiouchi comes before Gasquet on the river climb. Near the summit, the Middle Fork turns east while the highway follows Griffin Creek toward the tunnel. Beyond it, the road descends beside Broken Kettle Creek into Elk Valley before crossing into Oregon.

moments.title: Jedediah Smith Redwoods State Park
moments.text: The Smith River runs through a park established in 1929 to preserve old-growth redwoods. Its name recalls explorer Jedediah Smith’s passage through the area in 1826. The human history reaches much further back: archaeological evidence records more than 8,000 years of occupation. Tolowa people used the river and forest for resources, shelter, tools and cultural practices; their descendants live in the region and preserve traditions. The park also protects a spawning and migration route for fish in the Smith River. It is one of four parks managed together as Redwood National and State Parks.

moments.title: Gasquet
moments.text: At Gasquet, the North and Middle Forks join to form the Smith River. The town’s road history includes Mary Adams Peacock, who carried the mail between Crescent City and Grants Pass in the 1880s and 1890s. She also operated the Gasquet Village hotels, first under Gasquet family management and then on her own. The US 199 bridge across the Smith River near Gasquet received her name in 1932. The bridge had been built in 1926 and was remodeled in 1985. Nearby Adams Station, established by Peacock in 1898, served as a stagecoach stop.

moments.title: Collier Tunnel
moments.text: Collier Tunnel changed the summit crossing on July 20, 1963, replacing the winding road over Hazel View Summit with a route beneath it. The tunnel sits at about 2,100 feet, where the Smith River National Recreation Area meets Rogue River-Siskiyou National Forest. The old summit route survives as Oregon Mountain Road. Approaching from California, US 199 follows Griffin Creek after leaving the Middle Fork Smith River. On the other side, Broken Kettle Creek accompanies the descent toward Elk Valley and the Oregon line. The old Grants Pass–Crescent City route had been narrow and unpaved, with long grades.
